title: Love and Deepspace：失去信任的代价
content:
Love and Deepspace: The Price of Losing Trust
Skip to content
F2P Mobile
Love and Deepspace: The Price of Losing Trust
By Max Abrahamsen •   November 7, 2026
Source: Naavik
Love and Deepspace
(L&D) entered the mobile market with a bang, combining
otome
romance, RPG elements and action combat, wrapped in stunning visuals. Launched in January 2024 by Chinese publisher
Papergames
, it netted $265M in mobile revenue that year and $382M (+44% YoY) in 2025, despite falling downloads. This performance came while the broader RPG genre
was declining
.
Source:
Sensor Tower
, Naavik
In 2026, however, L&D’s commercial momentum reversed sharply.
From January to October 2026, revenue fell -47% YoY with average MAU dropping -10%. In other words, while L&D’s first two years tend to showcase how it turned high-fidelity RPG romance into a daily habit and great business, its third year exposes a divide between player needs and developer decisions.
In this article, we’ll explore how the game established itself as a juggernaut during its launch year, sustained its initial success the following year, why its growth engine weakened over 2026, and where the game’s trajectory might go from here. The data showcased excludes DTC, China Android, and ad revenue.
The Team and the Product
Source: Papergames
L&D was built on Papergames’ previous experience in developing games for women, from the
Nikki dress-up series
to 2017’s
Mr Love: Queen’s Choice
.
The team’s ambition was to make relationships feel more immediate through first-person 3D interaction and shared adventures. Introducing combat was one interpretation of shared adventures and reflected
a particular view of romance
: the heroine and her partner should face challenges as equals, building trust through mutual support. Fighting together was therefore part of the relationship itself, alongside everyday companionship. Delivering that vision required new capabilities.
Lizi Cheng (producer) recalls
that the original team lacked combat-development expertise and repeatedly rebuilt the system over four to five years.
Ultimately, that vision came together. Set in a future where hostile Wanderers threaten humanity after a mysterious message from Deepspace, L&D casts the player as a superpowered hunter who fights alongside men with whom she can develop romantic relationships.
Source: Love and Deepspace
The story, real-time battles and everyday companionship build relationships with a relatively small cast, supported by recurring content for favorite characters. Conversations, phone messages and date activities make those characters accessible between story releases, so attachment can develop through ordinary shared moments as well as major plot events. Story gates give combat development a purpose beyond harder challenges, while daily tasks help structure return visits.
Source: Love and Deepspace
L&D monetizes through a gacha system, where players draw collectible cards called Memories, each featuring a particular love interest. Memories strengthen combat teams, while some also unlock audio stories, interactive romantic scenes or chapters of longer Myth narratives. A desirable card can therefore appeal to players as both another experience with their favorite character and a useful addition to their team. Limited-time banners then concentrate that demand into short purchasing windows. Cosmetics, passes and resource purchases provide additional monetization.
Source: Naavik
2024: Satisfactory Launch Year Success
L&D’s $265M launch year unfolded in two stages: a launch surge that cooled through H1, followed by a second audience breakthrough and slightly improved monetization in H2. China supplied 63% of the year’s revenue, followed by the US and Japan at roughly 10% each.
Source:
Sensor Tower
, Naavik
H2 generated $166M, up +$67M (+68%) versus H1, with China supplying 66% of the increase and the US 17%. That translates into a +$358K/day improvement mainly driven by increases in existing-player activity (96%) and ARPDAU (11%), offset by a decrease in downloads (-7%).
Source:
Sensor Tower
, Naavik
H1: A satisfactory launch, followed by cooling.
Papergames launched with an audience cultivated through Nikki and Mr Love, preregistration campaigns, and localized promotion. Beyond 15M preregistrations, launch marketing efforts included
Sarah Brightman
’s theme song, regional creator activations,
a global PR push
, and
rewarded fan-content campaigns
. It also seems like significant UA spend was committed to launch, as Q1 downloads were 48% paid. That said, the game saw only 5.4M January downloads, equivalent to 36% of worldwide preregistrations. While accounting for China Android installs would push this ratio up, we’d guess less than optimal preregistration campaign performance since roughly half of the launch month downloads came from paid UA too.
By Q2, downloads settled around 360K monthly, while average MAU fell an additional -22% versus Q1 to 3.5M. Even though some banner events like Rafayel’s
When Tides Echo
, Xavier’s
Shimmering Moonlight
and Zayne’s
Trace of Divinity
drove opening day ARPDAU peaks of around $3 (versus Q1’s $2 maximum), quarterly average ARPDAU was slightly lower at $0.63 (vs $0.67). Quarterly revenue reached $45.8M (-14% QoQ), driven by lower download volume.
H2: A second audience breakthrough, followed by stronger monetization.
July 15’s
major v2.0 release
introduced Sylus, a fourth love interest whose outlaw persona broadened the romantic cast, alongside more story, roguelike combat, and higher progression caps. Marketing efforts included
a July 6 preview broadcast
,
a Mozart, l’opéra rock theme-song collaboration
and
IRL pop-up events
. July downloads rebounded to 2.0M versus Q2’s monthly baseline of roughly 360K, while Q3’s average MAU grew +38% to 4.8M. Since paid UA supplied 29% of July’s and 25% of Q3’s downloads versus 48% in Q1, it’s likely that Sylus’ arrival gave lapsed players a plausible reason to return alongside organically acquired newco
